h1: The 5 Best Monochrome Laser Printers for Home Offices of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Mono Laser Printers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: two true mono laser printers plus three close alternatives for home offices, compared on duplex, wireless, toner and price.
mainKeyword: monochrome laser printer for home office
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best monochrome laser for a home office, with wireless, duplex and separate drum and toner. The HP LaserJet M209d is the cheaper wired option. The Brother HL-L3220CDW and Canon MF753Cdw II are color lasers for occasional color or busy scanning, and the HP OfficeJet Pro 9135 is the inkjet contrast.
intro: Search results for mono laser printers blur three different machines together: true black-and-white lasers, color lasers and inkjets. Buyers end up paying for color capability they never use, or for inkjet cartridges that clog in the weeks between jobs. A text-heavy office wants a laser engine because toner is a dry powder that keeps for months, and a black-only model stops buying three cartridges it will not touch.

The awkward truth of this ranking is supply. Only two printers in our pool are real monochrome lasers, so the list adds two color lasers that handle black and white well and one inkjet as a contrast, and each pick is labeled for what it is. We ranked five on spec sheets: engine type, duplex, wireless, toner design and price tier.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: A true mono laser with wireless, duplex and separate drum and toner.
products.description:
The Brother DCP-L2640DW is a true mono laser that does the practical things well. It prints black only with a laser engine, handles two-sided jobs automatically, accepts wireless and phone printing, and keeps the drum and toner as separate parts. Separate parts mean you usually replace only the toner, and the drum lasts through several of them, which is why cost per page stays low.

It ranks above the HP M209d because it adds wireless and a lower long-term cost from the split design. Brother also tends to accept off-brand toner, which can reduce running expense. It sits in the $200 to $500 bucket.

Buy it for regular document volume. The caveat is the higher upfront price, and a compact paper capacity that suits a home office more than a busy one.

products.name: HP LaserJet M209d Laser Printer, Black and White
products.verdict: A cheaper mono laser, wired only.
products.description:
The HP LaserJet M209d is the budget mono laser. It prints black and white with a laser engine and automatic duplex, and connects by a plain USB cable, with a warm-up of roughly ten to fifteen seconds from cold. For a desk with a computer next to it, that is all the printer you need, in the $100 to $200 bucket.

It ranks below the Brother because it lacks wireless, so phones and laptops cannot print without a cable. It costs less, which is its whole case.

Buy it for a desk with a printer cable nearby and mostly text jobs. The caveat is toner: HP firmware can restrict off-brand cartridges, which raises running costs over time, so budget for original toner. If you print from a phone, the Brother is the better buy.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Wireless Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: Not mono-only, but a good fit for mostly black-and-white offices that sometimes need color.
products.description:
The Brother HL-L3220CDW is the first of the non-mono picks, and it earns its place for a mostly black-and-white office that sometimes needs a color page. It prints color and black, runs at about 19 pages per minute, holds 250 sheets and prints on both sides. Brother tends to accept off-brand toner, which keeps color refills from becoming a burden. It sits in the $200 to $500 bucket.

It ranks under the mono lasers because it does more than this guide's title asks, and color toner adds cost.

Choose it for mixed documents, such as invoices with a logo. The caveat is the extra consumables: three more toner cartridges to buy, even if you rarely use them, and a larger machine than a mono laser needs.
products.idealFor: Mostly B&W offices needing occasional color.

products.name: Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II Wireless Duplex Laser Printer
products.verdict: A fast all-in-one color laser with an auto document feeder.
products.description:
The Canon MF753Cdw II is a color laser multifunction built for volume. It feeds stacks through an automatic document feeder, prints about 35 pages a minute, keeps the drum apart from the toner and does two-sided printing over Wi-Fi. A fast engine and a feeder mean a stack of contracts or tax forms scans without babysitting.

It ranks below the Brother color laser on price and toner flexibility, because off-brand toner support is hit and miss. It prints nearly twice as fast, though, which matters for a busy room.

Buy it for a busier office that scans stacks. The caveat is that it is not a budget machine, in the $200 to $500 bucket, and a home user who prints a page a day will pay for capability they never use. Choose a mono laser instead for light work.

products.name: HP OfficeJet Pro 9135 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: An inkjet for offices that want a feeder and fax, not laser economics.
products.description:
The HP OfficeJet Pro 9135 is the inkjet contrast. It uses ink rather than toner, and adds an automatic document feeder, duplex printing and scanning, fax-ready features, and a 3-month Instant Ink trial. It prints color easily and scans two-sided pages, which lasers at this size rarely do.

It ranks last because it misses the mono laser brief. It shows the alternative: easier color and a better feature set, with ink that can dry out if the printer sits unused. That is the tradeoff against toner, which stays usable for long idle periods.

Choose it if features matter more than per-page cost. The caveat is that inkjet economics differ from laser, and a light user will lose ink to cleaning cycles. For a text-heavy office, the Brother DCP-L2640DW is the better fit.
products.idealFor: Offices that value features over laser economics.

whatMatters.detail: Mono lasers use a single black toner and cost less to run than color lasers, which carry three more. If you rarely print color, a mono laser wastes nothing. Check the engine type in the title, and note that some listings say laser while hiding that the machine prints color. Read the full title, not just the first words.

A separate drum lets you replace only toner most of the time, which lowers cost per page. All-in-one cartridges throw away the drum with every refill. Check the listing for a split design, as the Brother DCP-L2640DW and Canon MF753Cdw II list, and for the drum's rated life, since a short-lived drum erases the saving.

Some firmware blocks off-brand toner, which raises running costs and can leave you stuck if original cartridges are out of stock. Look for notes on third-party tolerance. Brother is generally tolerant, HP firmware may block it, and the Canon is hit and miss, so read owner reports first and keep a spare original cartridge.

Automatic duplex halves paper use and gives tidier handouts, while manual duplex needs you to flip pages and is slower. Check for automatic duplex in the title or bullets, and confirm that scanning is duplex too if you plan to digitize two-sided documents, since that is a separate feature that many laser models lack. Scan duplex is mostly a feeder feature.

Wireless lets phones and laptops print without cables, and USB-only models need a nearby computer. Check connectivity in the title. A wired printer is simple and reliable, but it ties printing to one machine, so decide whether you will print from a phone before you pick the cheaper model, then check the mobile app exists.

faq.q: Why are only two printers true mono lasers?
faq.a: Our pool contained only two. The rest are color lasers or inkjets that appear in related searches, and we label them clearly so you can see the difference and decide whether color or a feeder is worth it. Four labeled alternatives follow the two true mono lasers.
Buying a color laser they use only for black text, then paying for four toners. A true mono laser such as the Brother DCP-L2640DW needs just one, and the toner lasts longer.

faq.q: Is a mono laser worth over an inkjet?
faq.a: For text-heavy offices, yes. Toner lasts and does not dry out, so an idle laser works on the first page after weeks, while the OfficeJet may waste ink on a cleaning cycle before it prints.

faq.q: How do I set up wireless?
faq.a: Use the printer's panel or app to join your Wi-Fi, then add it on your device. The HP M209d has no wireless, so it connects by USB cable only; keep it near your computer.

faq.q: How do I maintain a laser?
faq.a: Replace toner when prompted, and the drum when quality fades. On the Brother and Canon, the drum is a separate part. Keep paper dry and the paper path clear of scraps, and use fresh paper to avoid jams.

Brother is generally tolerant, HP firmware may block it, and the Canon is hit and miss, so check before buying. Original toner is the safe choice if you cannot test, even though it costs more per page.

finalTake: Buy the Brother DCP-L2640DW for steady document volume, or the HP M209d if a USB cable is fine and budget leads. Choose the Brother HL-L3220CDW when you sometimes need color, the Canon when stacks of scanning drive the day, and the OfficeJet only if features matter more than laser running costs.
